question: What is a priority entitlement supposed to do in federal public service staffing?
generated_answer: Priority entitlement is intended to provide certain groups of persons with better access to employment in the public service, as a way of addressing disadvantages in employment experienced by members of those groups. You have been given priority entitlement in this appointment process because you have self-declared as an Indigenous person. If you have self-declared as an Indigenous person and you have been assessed by the Public Service Commission as meeting the essential qualifications for the appointment process, you will be referred to the deputy head for appointment ahead of non-priority candidates who otherwise have an equal or higher rating than you. In other words, you have been given priority over non-Indigenous candidates with an equal or higher rating than you. You may be appointed ahead of a non-priority candidate with a higher rating than you if the deputy head determines that doing so is in compliance with the Public Service Employment Act. Priority entitlement does not constitute a right to appointment. It is the deputy head who makes the appointment decision, and you must meet the essential qualifications for the position. Deputy heads are also expected to take steps to identify and remove barriers in staffing processes to ensure fairness and equity in staffing. For more information about priority entitlement, please consult the Public Service Commission’s Priority Entitlements webpages. Do I have to self-declare as an Indigenous person in order to receive priority entitlement? You are not required to self-declare as an Indigenous person. Self-declaration is voluntary. However, if you do not self-declare as an Indigenous person, you will not receive priority entitlement. What if I don’t self-declare as an Indigenous person? If you do not self-declare as an Indigenous person, you will not receive priority entitlement. If you do not self-declare, you will be considered to be a non-priority candidate. What if I self-declare as an Indigenous person but I am assessed as not meeting the essential qualifications for the appointment process? If you self-declare as an Indigenous person but you are assessed by the Public Service Commission as not meeting the essential qualifications for the appointment process, you will not be eligible to receive priority entitlement. Do I need to provide proof of my Indigenous ancestry in order to receive priority entitlement? No. You are not required to provide proof of your Indigenous ancestry in order to receive priority entitlement. Self-declaration is sufficient. However, you should be aware that the Public Service Commission may ask you to provide proof of your Indigenous ancestry at a later date. If you are asked to provide proof of your Indigenous ancestry, you will be required to do so in order to maintain your priority entitlement. What are the essential qualifications for this appointment process? The essential qualifications for this appointment process are listed in the notice of opportunity. You must meet all of the essential qualifications in order to be eligible for priority entitlement. If you do not meet the essential qualifications, you will not be eligible for priority entitlement. Can I appeal the decision to grant or deny me priority entitlement? Yes. If you disagree with the decision to grant or deny you priority entitlement, you may appeal the decision to the Public Service Commission. For more information about the appeal process, please consult the Public Service Commission’s Priority Entitlements webpages.
